{{Short description|Problem about bus travel}}
[[File:Waiting for the bus 2765.jpg|thumb|right|Waiting girl sculpture at a bus stop in [[Aachen, Germany]]]]
The '''wait/walk dilemma''' occurs when waiting for a [[bus]] at a [[bus stop]], when the duration of the wait may exceed the time needed to arrive at a destination by another means, especially [[walking]].
Some work on this problem was featured in the 2008 "Year in Ideas" issue of ''The New York Times Magazine''.<ref name=Thompson>{{cite web
|url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2008/12/14/magazine/2008_IDEAS.html
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081214204356/http://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2008/12/14/magazine/2008_IDEAS.html
|url-status=dead
|archive-date=December 14, 2008
|title=The Bus-Wait Formula
|first=Clive
|last=Thompson
|publisher=The New York Times Magazine: Year in Ideas
|date=2008-12-13}}</ref>

==Research==
The dilemma has been studied in an unpublished report entitled "Walk Versus Wait: The Lazy Mathematician Wins."<ref name=Bierman>{{cite web
|url=http://archive.boston.com/news/local/articles/2008/02/03/cellphones_remain_mum_in_tunnels/
|title=Cellphones remain mum in tunnels
|first=Noah
|last=Bierman
|publisher=The Boston Globe
|date=2008-02-03}}</ref><ref name=NewSci>{{cite web
|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg19726404.600-lazy-option-is-best-when-waiting-for-the-bus.html
|title=Lazy option is best when waiting for the bus
|publisher=New Scientist Magazine
|date=2008-01-23}}</ref>  Anthony B. Morton's paper "A Note on Walking Versus Waiting" supports and extends Chen et al.'s results.<ref>{{cite arXiv
|eprint=0802.3653
|title=A Note on Walking Versus Waiting
|date=2008-02-25
|author1=Morton
|class=math.HO}}</ref> Ramnik Arora's "A Note on Walk versus Wait: Lazy Mathematician Wins" discusses what he believes to be some of the errors in Chen et al.'s argument; the result of Chen et al.'s paper still holds following Arora's alleged corrections.<ref>{{cite arXiv
|eprint=0803.3106
|title=A Note on Walk versus Wait: Lazy Mathematician Wins
|date=2008-03-21
|author1=Ramnik Arora
|class=math.HO}}</ref> As early as 1990, writer Tom Parker had observed that "walking is faster than waiting for a bus if you're going less than a mile".<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/79230732/ Excerpts from the book "Never Trust a Calm Dog and Other Rules of Thumb", as reproduced in the Gatesway Messenger]. May 22, 1996. Retrieved 9 November 2018</ref>

As an undergraduate mathematics major at [[Harvard]], Scott D. Kominers first began fixating on the problem while walking from [[MIT]] to [[Harvard]],<ref name=Bierman/> which are more than a mile apart in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]] along [[Route 1 (MBTA)|MBTA bus route 1]]. He enlisted the help of [[Caltech]] physics major Justin G. Chen and [[Harvard]] statistics major Robert W. Sinnott to perform the analysis.<ref name=Bierman/>

Their paper concludes that it is usually mathematically quicker to wait for the bus{{Dubious|Dubious conclusion|date=July 2018}}, at least for a little while.<!-- A little while isn't even a number --> But once made, the decision to walk should be final instead of waiting again at subsequent stops.<ref name=Bierman/><ref name=Thompson/> The paper also showed potential applications to the field of cryptography.

==Interstellar travel==
The corresponding problem in interstellar travel is called the [[wait calculation]], which tries to determine the optimal time to wait for technological progress to improve spaceship speeds before committing to the journey.
